extracted.intended_audience: General readers researching philanthropy, grantmakers, donors, and those interested in Coefficient Giving/Open Philanthropy's grantmaking approach
extracted.subtask_description: Describes Coefficient Giving's (formerly Open Philanthropy) criteria, processes, and heuristics for selecting causes, estimating impact, and allocating grant funding across programs and funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance
rubrics_metrics.description: How many individuals are affected by the problem, and how deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of three core cause-selection criteria Coefficient Giving uses when choosing focus areas. Importance is evaluated alongside neglectedness and tractability as part of 'strategic cause selection.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the cause receives adequate attention and resources from others, especially other major philanthropists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the three core cause-selection criteria. A cause that is highly neglected (relative to its scale) is more attractive because additional funding is likely to have higher marginal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tractability
rubrics_metrics.description: The likelihood that a philanthropic funder can contribute to significant progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the three core cause-selection criteria. Tractability considers whether practical interventions or funding can plausibly move the needle on the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic cause selection (large, tractable, neglected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select focus areas by looking for problems that are large, tractable, and neglected relative to their size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cause looks promising according to those criteria, researchers review literature and meet with experts to better understand the area, then conduct an investigation to determine whether there are enough strong giving opportunities to justify opening a new program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-opening investigation / sufficient giving opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Before opening a new program, conduct detailed investigation to determine whether there are enough strong giving opportunities to justify a program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigation steps described include literature review, expert meetings, and more detailed project-level evaluation; the organization will only open a program if investigations indicate sufficient promising opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact estimation (quantitative, back-of-the-envelope calculations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantitative approaches — for example, back-of-the-envelope calculations based on scientific evidence — to estimate a grant's expected impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coefficient Giving often uses these quick quantitative estimates to evaluate projects in areas like vaccine research, farm animal welfare, and development of environmental lead detection techniques. Guidance includes grounding estimates in best-available scientific evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hits-based giving (high-risk, high-reward)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue 'high-risk, high-reward' opportunities that may lack strong evidence or a high chance of success but could produce enormous positive impact if they succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is explicitly compared to venture-capital-style strategies. Coefficient Giving cites historical philanthropic 'hits' (e.g., the Green Revolution, oral contraceptives) and gives examples such as early support for basic science (David Baker's protein design work) as instances where high uncertainty was tolerated for potential outsized payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalize marginal returns across interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to equalize marginal returns across different interventions to maximize overall impact across the portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across the portfolio, the organization seeks to allocate resources so that marginal return (impact per additional dollar) is balanced across funded interventions — a portfolio-level allocation principle rather than a per-grant metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of focused funds pooling multiple donors
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize work across focused funds that pool money from multiple donors, each dedicated to a particular area and directed toward the most promising opportunities in that area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coefficient Giving's work is split across multiple funds (13 at time of article). Each fund pools donor money and targets opportunities the organization judges most promising; launching a fund follows the cause-selection/investigation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for evidence-backed interventions in global health & wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Support 'evidence-backed interventions' to improve health and wellbeing (e.g., malaria prevention, routine vaccinations, scaling water chlorination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Global Health & Wellbeing Opportunities program explicitly funds interventions with supporting evidence and scales interventions where evidence indicates cost-effective impact. Notable grantees are cited as examples of this evidence-focused funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for forecasting quality and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fund efforts that enable the creation of high-quality forecasts on questions relevant to high-stakes decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Forecasting program funds platforms and researchers (e.g., Philip Tetlock, Metaculus) that improve forecasting accuracy and supply decision-relevant probabilistic predictions to inform grantmaking and policy prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for work on global catastrophic risks and foundational capacity-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Fund cross-cutting and foundational work to build capacity for addressing global catastrophic risks (GCRs), including enabling people to work full-time on mitigation and expanding academic/educational capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fund prioritizes projects that create durable, cross-cutting capacity (e.g., course development, hiring people into GCR work) even if specific near-term interventions are less obvious; notable grantees include CEAs and academics developing courses.
